lesson.title: When to refer out
lesson.summary: Referral is a coaching skill: notice, stop, refer to the right place at the right speed, and keep the client training what is safe.
objectives: Apply the three referral tiers, with the highest matching tier winning.
Use the stop rules and say what to do next.
Know who is outside the base module and how to work alongside a clinician's plan.
Refer in plain, calm, non-diagnostic words.

blocks.content: Every lesson in this module has put a stop-and-refer box beside its screens and progressions. This lesson puts them all in one place. The lists below come straight from Spindle's shoulder safety rules.
A trainer does not diagnose or treat injuries. A trainer notices, stops, and refers. Describe what you see, never name a condition, and never tell a client a screen has cleared them.

content.label: Spindle policy
content.text: Your training is not treatment for a diagnosed condition. A client with diagnosed shoulder pain, or one recovering from surgery, a dislocation or a fracture, trains within the treating clinician's plan, and you do not progress that plan on your own. This is Spindle's rule for trainers, not a research finding.

blocks.content: Which tier: the highest one that matches
Use the highest tier that any sign matches. An emergency sign overrides every urgent or routine sign, and an urgent sign overrides every routine sign.
Emergency: call emergency services now (999 in the UK)

content: Chest pain that feels tight, crushing or squeezing, or chest pain that spreads to the arm, neck or jaw; severe difficulty breathing; the person collapses or does not respond normally

After an injury (a fall, an impact, a joint that "popped out", a seizure or an electric shock), the client cannot move the arm, or the shoulder looks out of place or has changed shape. Do not move the arm or try to put it back. Do not let the client drive themselves.
Signs of a joint infection: the shoulder is suddenly very painful and red or warm, or the client has a fever or feels unwell with shoulder pain

content.label: Note on infection
content.text: the NHS shoulder pain page lists fever or feeling unwell, and an arm that is hot or cold to the touch, as urgent reasons to get help. Spindle's rule is deliberately stricter for fever or feeling unwell: a trainer cannot tell whether a joint is infected, and BESS asks for same-day emergency referral when infection is suspected. That stricter mapping is Spindle policy. A shoulder that feels hot or cold to the touch, or is badly swollen, without sudden severe pain, redness, fever or feeling unwell, stays urgent.

blocks.content: Urgent: an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 today (or the local equivalent)

content: Sudden or very bad shoulder pain
New loss of active movement without an injury: the client cannot lift or move the arm themselves, even if it can be moved for them

After an injury, pain and weakness, while the arm still moves and the shoulder looks normal (possible acute cuff tear). BESS asks for urgent specialist assessment at the next available clinic; its 2014 guide gives under 2 weeks.
Any other new shoulder pain that started after an injury or accident, such as a fall
The arm or shoulder has changed shape or is badly swollen, with no injury and no sign of infection
Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling in the arm or shoulder
The arm or shoulder feels hot or cold to the touch, with no sign of infection (no sudden severe pain with redness or warmth, no fever, not unwell)
Severe pain in both shoulders
A new lump, mass or swelling around the shoulder
New pain, swelling or stiffness in several joints at once
A child or adolescent with shoulder pain: urgent GP or NHS 111 the same day, for referral to trauma and orthopaedics; tell a parent or carer
Shoulder pain that is getting worse. Refer now; do not wait for 2 weeks to pass.
Shoulder pain that is not getting worse but has not improved after 2 weeks
Moving the arm or shoulder is very difficult, but the client can still move it themselves
Pain and stiffness that do not go away, including pain that is worse at night
Pain that persists after the trainer has removed the provoking movements

blocks.content: Stop always means no further loading of that shoulder in this session. Changes to range, load or variation belong to a later session, and only if no warning sign remains.

content: Pain comes on or rises with load, or a movement seems to make the shoulder worse - Stop shoulder loading for this session. If the pain is getting worse, routine referral now: there is no need to wait. If it is not getting worse but has not improved after 2 weeks, routine referral.
Numbness, pins and needles, or loss of feeling in the arm or shoulder - Stop. Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling, is urgent.
After an injury, the client cannot move the arm, or the shoulder looks out of place or has changed shape - Stop. Do not move the arm or try to put it back. Emergency.

New loss of active movement: the client cannot lift or move the arm themselves (even if you could move it for them), without an injury - Stop. Urgent. Never treat this as a mobility or control problem to train.
After an injury, pain and weakness, but the arm still moves and the shoulder looks normal - Stop. Urgent (possible acute cuff tear).
Signs of a joint infection: the shoulder is suddenly very painful and red or warm, or the client has a fever or feels unwell with shoulder pain - Stop. Emergency.
Arm pain together with chest pain, tightness, breathlessness, or feeling faint - Stop all exercise. Emergency: call emergency services.
Pain at night that wakes the client, with stiffness that is not going away - Do not progress shoulder loading. Routine.
Recent injury or accident, such as a fall, with new shoulder pain that has not been assessed - Do not train the shoulder. Use the referral tiers above.
After shoulder surgery, or a recent dislocation or fracture, still in rehabilitation - Outside the base module. Follow the treating clinician's plan; do not progress it on your own.
Diagnosed neurological condition affecting the arm or neck - Outside the base module.
Diagnosed shoulder condition under current care (for example frozen shoulder, a known cuff tear, instability) - Outside the base module; work only within the clinician's plan.

Children and adolescents with shoulder pain - Outside the base module. Urgent tier: stop shoulder loading, and tell the young person and their parent or carer to get an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 (or the local equivalent) the same day, for referral to trauma and orthopaedics. Emergency tier if any emergency criterion applies.
Anyone with a warning sign in the lists above - Stop and refer.

blocks.content: For subacromial shoulder pain, UK specialist guidance describes the condition as usually self-limiting, with most symptoms settling within about three months.
That keeps a routine referral calm. It is about one diagnosed condition, and it never delays an urgent or emergency referral.

content: Say what you saw: "Your arm isn't lifting as high as last week, and that's new."
Say what to do and how soon: "That's worth getting checked today by a GP or NHS 111."
Do not name a condition, and do not say it is nothing.
Keep them moving where it is safe: "Let's work on your lower body for the rest of the session."

blocks.content: Ask the client to share the plan, ideally in writing. Train within it, ask the clinician before changing it, and do not progress it on your own.

content.prompt: For subacromial shoulder pain, what does UK specialist guidance say about how symptoms usually go?
options: Most symptoms settle within about three months
content.explanation: The guidance describes subacromial pain as usually self-limiting, with most symptoms settling within about three months.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: Pick the tier and say what you do first: (1) arm pain with chest tightness during a session; (2) a new lump above the collarbone; (3) shoulder pain that has got worse every day this week, with no other sign; (4) after a fall, the client cannot move the arm; (5) fever and shoulder pain; (6) an ache after training that settled within a day, with no other sign.
